Messages.Author: Jon
Messages.Body:
I am seeking an answer to the question of order of play - specifically on
Bleed modifiers.

Lets say I am bled for 1 blood by my predator. I have reaction card
telepathic misdirection but I am not gonna waste it on a 1 blood loss.

Predator then ups the bleed to 4

Question 1 - when do I play my misdirection - after declared bleed action,
after declared bleed or after that bleed has been modified ?

Question 2 - if i successfully re-direct I presume that any Stealth applied
still stands ?

Question 3 - can that redirected bleed be re-directed back to me using the
same card (telepathic redirection) ?

Okay a quick question. When can you play an action modifier? Do you only get
"one chance" at playing cards?

Let me try to clarify that last sentence. A long long time ago (when I still
played M:TG), there was some story about how some person attacked with a
creature. The attacker then asked if the defender wanted to play anything in
response and the defender declined. The attacking player then tried to play a
card (an Instant), but a judge said that by asking if the defending player
wants to play anything, it means he can't do anything more (UNLESS the
defending player plays something as well, and then the attacker can respond to
that).

I know that was a Magic example, but then again, they were WotC games for
awhile and all.

So my question is when do I have to play my action modifiers? If I bleed with a
vampire, what happens if (or when) I ask the opposing player if he wants to
play a reaction? (Though the smart player will just respond with a "maybe" or
something). And BTW, is the prey bound to whatever he answers (I'd say not)?

Halcyan 2

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Halcyan 2 wrote:
>
> > "Question 1 - when do I play my misdirection - after declared bleed
> >action, after declared bleed or after that bleed has been modified?"
> >
> >Whenever you want, it's your reaction. Read that as before or after you
> >declare a block.
>
> Okay a quick question. When can you play an action modifier? Do you only get
> "one chance" at playing cards?

At any time.
You get a new opportunity every time anything happens (like right
after you play an action modifier, or after a reaction card is
played, or after "no block" is declared, etc.)

> Let me try to clarify that last sentence. A long long time ago (when I still
> played M:TG), there was some story about how some person attacked with a
> creature. The attacker then asked if the defender wanted to play anything in
> response and the defender declined. The attacking player then tried to play a
> card (an Instant), but a judge said that by asking if the defending player
> wants to play anything, it means he can't do anything more (UNLESS the
> defending player plays something as well, and then the attacker can respond to
> that).

Right.
If you (the acting player) say "do you want to play something", that means
you are opting not to play anything at this time. If no one else does
anything, then that's it.

This solves certain timing problems that would lead to stalemates of
activity.

A: "Vamp1 bleeds you, B"
<opportunity for A to play cards/effects>
A: "Do you block?"
<indicates that A has no other effects to play at this time>
B: "I don't block"
<opportunity for A to play cards/effects>
A: "OK, do you deflect or anything?"
<indicates that A has no other effects to play at this time>
B: "No"
<since everyone has declined to play any more effects, the
action resolves>

B loses 1 pool.

> I know that was a Magic example, but then again, they were WotC games for
> awhile and all.
>
> So my question is when do I have to play my action modifiers? If I bleed with a
> vampire, what happens if (or when) I ask the opposing player if he wants to
> play a reaction?

Since you (the acting player) always have the first opportunity to play
an effect, asking for a reaction indicates that you do not wish to play
any effects at that time. If no one else does anything, then that's that.
If, however, anyone else plays an effect, the opportunity to play the
next effect again falls to you first.

>(Though the smart player will just respond with a "maybe" or
> something). And BTW, is the prey bound to whatever he answers (I'd say not)?

This is the problematic situation being avoided.
